To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the number of inertia sensors and their location on the human body have an impact on the recognition of human activities and postures and that the use of quaternion-based approaches is a promising solution to improve the recognition performance.
the use of raw data from a single IMMU, placed at the lower back, thigh, or foot locations, leads to more than 80 % of the activities and poses being correctly classified.
the proposed algorithm is efficient to recognize human activities and postures using only one IMMU placed on the back, the left foot, or the left thigh.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the recognition of human activities and postures using a minimum number of IMMUs, which can be used for the development of wearable systems.
two main contributions: the use of raw data in the recognition process, and the use of attitude, in term quaternion, to achieve the recognition process.

two main objectives: 1. to investigate the effect of the placement of inertial sensors on the recognition of human activities and postures, and 2. to investigate the use of quaternion in order to more accurately assess the effect of placement of inertial sensor on recognition.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
using quaternion is a better approach to recognize human activities and postures than using raw data from IMMUs.

the use of raw data is a simple but efficient way to recognize human postures and activity and that the attitude of a body segment can be used as a feature to improve the recognition accuracy, especially when the number of IMMUs is limited.
the use of quaternion, in term of orientation and attitude, in addition to raw data from accelerometers and gyroscopes, is the best approach for human posture and activity recognition.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
using quaternion instead of raw data, with only one IMMU placed on the lower thigh, leads to a better performance in terms of accuracy and computational time.

, in the context of the recognition of human activities and postures, the use of raw data from inertial sensors can lead to good recognition rates, but the extraction of attitude from inertial sensors, and the use of quaternion as features, significantly improves the accuracy of the classifier.
, for the studied activities, the use of a single IMMU, with a placement on the lower back or left thigh, is enough to recognize the activities and posture.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the number of sensors used in human activity recognition can be reduced to a single sensor and that the placement of the sensor on the lower back is sufficient for most of the studied activities.
, in terms of accuracy and computational complexity, the use of a single sensor placed on the lower part of the body, such as on the left thigh, is the most suitable solution.
using a smaller subset of sensors, placed on specific body segments (lower back, left thigh and left foot), can achieve a high accuracy for the recognition of activities and postures.
